You walk into a room and the weights become visible — what's owed, what isn't, who's carrying something that wasn't theirs to pick up. When you account for how you got that, you credit the situation. Anyone would notice, you say. But the reading is yours, and it's good, and the fact that it's quiet doesn't make it borrowed. Privacy is part of how it works. What's unclaimed is your name on it. Put your own mark on the read and the next one comes through clearer. You're not deciding anything here, just sorting whose weight is whose.
4.sheetLine: You see what's fair here. You file it under circumstance.

1.tense: You are here with the pen now, and the account is being kept cleanly.
1.verb: keeping the private account of what is fair
1.place: the wide view where the whole pattern shows at once
1.ask: Take something that ended in the past year and, over a few lines in your own hand, set out what it left you. Note whether it changes what you do next — or that it doesn't.
1.core: When the whole pattern is visible at once, you can still feel what is owed. A thing ends, and you can look at what it left behind and count it plainly, without making more or less of it. The count holds because you saw the ending through instead of outrunning it, and what came of it is sitting there to be taken in. Others look at the same field and go cold or go soft. You look, and the fairness survives the view. That is the ground under you right now, and it is being used rather than guarded. The waiting produced something you can name, and naming it is the whole of the next step.
1.sheetLine: You see the whole field, and the account comes out fair.

2.tense: You are bracing at a future that cannot be written in, and the account is running ahead of what has happened.
2.verb: keeping the private account of what is fair
2.place: the wide view where the whole pattern shows at once
2.ask: Hand one person a real piece of help they are short on — something you have plenty of — and finish it before the week ends. Then stop; no follow-up.
2.core: When the whole pattern is visible, every uneven edge of it shows at once, and you are settling all of them before they arrive. What should be a clear knowing of what is fair has become a running total of what will be owed, and the total keeps you up above the room. People can feel that you have already decided how it comes out, and they stop bringing you their half of it. Fairness moves through a room without you doing the sums when the thing is working. Aim your strength at one real shortage, finish it, and stop before the tally starts. The help need not be small to be finished in a week, only finished.
2.sheetLine: You are settling accounts that have not happened yet.

3.tense: You are still standing at a door that is already behind you, and the wide view is not being used.
3.verb: keeping the private account of what is fair
3.place: the wide view where the whole pattern shows at once
3.ask: Next time someone near you is stuck on a decision, describe the route you can see from where you sit, out loud, before you talk yourself out of it.
3.core: You can see the whole pattern and you are not saying what you see. What you read stays private and unwritten, and from outside it looks like nothing is being weighed. The passage you can see is not being named, and others walk past it. Sight, not feeling, is what is missing here. A clear read of a situation offered plainly is not judgement — it is just the view from where you stand, and it takes nothing away from the person who needs it. The read has not left you; it has stopped coming out. Saying the route aloud is the smallest thing this does when it is working.
3.sheetLine: You see the whole pattern and are saying none of it.

4.tense: The pen is down in a room you are already writing in, and the account is being kept without your name.
4.verb: keeping the private account of what is fair
4.place: the wide view where the whole pattern shows at once
4.ask: Take a sheet of paper and set out everything pulling at you right now — then mark beside each one whether it is yours or something you picked up from someone. Keep the sheet.
4.core: You have been reading the whole pattern for a while and calling it what is obviously true. When something is off, you state it as though anyone would see the same thing, and it usually turns out you are right. Direct knowing lands without argument when the thing is working, and being comfortable not knowing is part of it. Right now what you see is steering things and being filed as plain fact, so nobody, including you, thinks to put your name on it. A borrowed pull and a real one look identical from the wide view. Marking which is which takes a page and a few minutes.
4.sheetLine: You read the whole pattern and call it plain fact.

2.tense: The verdict on this ending will be ready long before the ending is.
2.verb: weighing what feels fair against what is
2.place: where completion opens rather than closes
2.ask: Carry one concrete errand for somebody this week and stop the moment it's finished. Nothing gets added on after.
2.core:
The compass is out running in front of the road. Something in you has already called how this finish will land, and that call is being used to hold the rest steady. What it looks like is pre-accounting — settling what will be owed, and by whom, while the thing is still open. The tightness isn't dishonesty. It's a body braced for a judgment nobody has asked it to make yet.

Strength shared is what takes the weight off. Carry one concrete thing for someone — an errand, a run, a piece that finishes — where the only point is that it got done, not that it got balanced. That's how you remember strength can be contained instead of drawn tight across all of what's coming. It isn't the real close. It's proof that some things hold without pulling.
2.sheetLine: You're calling the verdict before the chapter ends.

3.tense: A verdict was reached, and the door it belonged to is already behind you.
3.verb: weighing what feels fair against what is
3.place: where completion opens rather than closes
3.ask: Do one stretch of the thing alongside somebody stuck in it. Go at their pace, stop when they stop, and don't correct the way they're doing it.
3.core:
Some decision about this ending got made — what was fair, what's owed, who came out short — and that decision left you standing outside the finish. The route is still yours; you're just not on it. Fairness has gone quiet and turned into auditing old accounts, so the chapter sits open in your hands and nothing new arrives.

The way through isn't to feel fair again. It's to spend what you know on someone else's behalf. Walk a piece of it beside someone who's stuck in the same place, at the pace they set, and let where it ends be theirs. You're not closing the chapter by doing this. You're keeping the channel clear while the part of you that can feel a verdict catches up to the one that pronounced it. That's the whole of the job today.
3.sheetLine: A verdict was reached and the doorway is behind you.

4.tense: The compass is steering, and the hand on it is not fully in the room.
4.verb: weighing what feels fair against what is
4.place: where completion opens rather than closes
4.ask: Put the rules you're judging this ending by on a page, a line for each. Circle the borrowed ones, then look at the circles once a day for a week.
4.core:
The finish is being steered by a sense of what's fair, and that sense is being reported as something else — mood, tiredness, or a logic that got picked up along the way. The steering is yours. The story of it isn't, and the gap matters, because a chapter closed by rules you didn't choose will feel tidy and hollow at the same time.

Sorting what's yours from what you took on is what closes the gap. Get the rules you've been judging this stretch by onto a page, a line for each, and mark which ones you chose. You don't have to throw the others out. You just have to see where each one came from. Keep the ones that are yours, and the ending gets closed by you instead of an old borrowed voice.
4.sheetLine: You're steering by rules you didn't write.
